qs.q: : Platelet Activating Factor (PAF) is chemically classified as a
qs.e: PAF is chemically acetyl-glyceryl-ether-phosphocholine, making it a phospholipid derivative. Despite its small size compared to eicosanoids, it has potent biological activities including platelet aggregation, inflammation, and increased vascular permeability at very low concentrations (nanomolar range).

faq.a: PAF activates platelets (promoting clotting) while simultaneously increasing vascular permeability, which can lead to bleeding into tissues.
faq.q: Why does PAF cause both clotting and bleeding?

faq.a: Direct measurement requires specialized lipidomics not available in most low‑resource labs; clinicians infer its activity from clinical pattern.
Steroids are used when the reaction is moderate‑to‑severe or when an allergic trigger is suspected; mild, self‑limited reactions may resolve with supportive care alone.

exam: A patient with sudden wheeze after cleaning cotton sacks – what immediate steps do you take and why? — Assess airway, give high‑flow oxygen, start bronchodilator, give IV fluids; consider steroids to block PAF.
How does PAF differ from histamine in causing shock? — PAF adds platelet activation and profound capillary leak, while histamine mainly causes vasodilation.

In a malaria‑endemic area, a febrile child develops sudden hypotension – which mediator might be driving the crisis and what drug class would you avoid? — PAF from infected erythrocytes; avoid NSAIDs that can worsen platelet dysfunction.
Explain why a normal CRP does not rule out severe PAF‑mediated anaphylaxis. — CRP rises later; early shock is driven by mediator release, not cytokine synthesis.
What bedside sign helps you differentiate PAF‑driven bronchospasm from pneumonia? — Reversible wheeze that improves with bronchodilator versus crackles and consolidation on auscultation.
When PAF‑receptor antagonists are unavailable, what is the next best pharmacologic strategy? — Systemic corticosteroids to inhibit upstream phospholipase A2 and reduce PAF synthesis.
List three common tropical exposures that can trigger PAF release. — Cotton dust, biomass smoke, bacterial infections (e.g., TB, malaria).

A patient on herbal remedy develops urticaria and hypotension – how do you assess whether PAF is involved? — Look for rapid onset after exposure, platelet activation signs, and response to steroids; consider stopping the herb.
ai.title: Platelet Activating Factor
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Platelet‑activating factor (PAF) is a potent phospholipid mediator that drives platelet aggregation, vascular leakage, and leukocyte activation in inflammation and allergy. Understanding its triggers, clinical clues, and limited investigations helps clinicians manage acute and chronic inflammatory states, especially where resources are scarce.

b: No single bedside test; diagnosis is clinical, based on context of inflammation or allergic reaction.
sections.p: PAF is a bioactive lipid released by activated cells (platelets, neutrophils, endothelial cells) that binds the PAF receptor to trigger aggregation, vasodilation, and leukocyte recruitment.

b: Mild: localized reaction (e.g., skin rash, mild bronchospasm).
Moderate: systemic symptoms (fever, widespread urticaria, mild hypotension).
Severe: anaphylaxis‑like picture, shock, acute lung injury.
sections.p: Severity is judged by the extent of systemic inflammation and organ involvement rather than a formal stage.

b: Inhaled irritants – cotton dust, smoke, biomass fuel.
Infections – malaria, TB, bacterial sepsis, HIV‑related opportunistic infections.
Allergens – insect stings, food allergens, herbal preparations.
Drug reactions – antibiotics (e.g., sulfonamides), NSAIDs.
sections.p: PAF release is triggered by many common insults in low‑resource settings.

b: Skin: flushing, urticaria, angio‑edema.
Respiratory: bronchoconstriction, wheeze, dyspnoea.
Cardiovascular: tachycardia, hypotension, capillary leak.
Gastro‑intestinal: abdominal pain, vomiting.
sections.p: Patients may present with a spectrum from mild allergic‑type symptoms to life‑threatening shock.
When a test is unavailable, rely on clinical scoring (e.g., shock index, respiratory rate) and treat empirically.

t.b: Is the patient in shock or developing respiratory failure? – Guides urgency of treatment.
Is there a systemic inflammatory response? – Elevated WBC/CRP supports infection or severe inflammation.
Is mast‑cell activation present? – High level suggests anaphylaxis where PAF is a co‑mediator.
Is there pulmonary infiltrate or edema? – Helps differentiate PAF‑driven lung injury from infection.

b: Progressive hypotension despite fluids.
Worsening bronchospasm unresponsive to bronchodilators.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
Multi‑organ failure.
sections.p: Uncontrolled PAF activity can precipitate rapid deterioration.

b: Remove exposure (e.g., stop cotton‑dust work, discontinue offending drug).
IV crystalloids for hypotension; consider colloids if capillary leak is severe.
Bronchodilators (salbutamol) for bronchospasm; oxygen therapy.
Corticosteroids (IV methylprednisolone) to inhibit phospholipase A2 and downstream PAF production.
Antihistamines for cutaneous symptoms; they do not block PAF but provide symptomatic relief.
Consider PAF‑receptor antagonists (e.g., ginkgolide B) only where available; avoid in pregnancy.
sections.p: Treat the trigger, then blunt PAF‑mediated effects.

b: Educate patients on protective masks when handling cotton or biomass.
Vaccinate against common infections (influenza, pneumococcus).
Review drug history; avoid known sensitizers.
Monitor for late sequelae such as asthma or chronic urticaria.
sections.p: After acute control, identify and avoid recurrent triggers.

b: Histamine – causes vasodilation but less platelet aggregation.
Leukotriene C4/D4 – bronchoconstriction without strong platelet effects.
Thromboxane A2 – platelet aggregation without prominent vascular leak.
sections.p: PAF effects overlap with other mediators.

b: Normal CRP does not exclude severe PAF‑mediated shock.
Serum tryptase may be normal if sampling is delayed beyond 2 h.
